title: Guidance colorizing values within a column
description:
I'm excited about this package, and am hopeful it might fit my needs.

I'm trying to colorize values within a column - I have logic, functions, methods I can use to colorize values in a column. I do not see how to apply this logic.

The simplest use case is to colorize positive numeric values blue, since negative is red.
Similarly, I have categorical colors, how might I apply them to a `character` column?

Best guess, I need to write custom functions to override `pillar:::pillar_shaft.classname()` for every column class, by the class of data in each column.

Is there another way to inject color into the output?

The vignette/extensions does not describe where to inject color. The custom Body function does receive column values, however they are `pillar_component` objects which contain data values in the form of (undocumented) `pillar_ornament` object. I think these values have already been updated by a previous `pillar_shaft()` step.

In the vctrs package, the vignette `"Printing vectors nicely in tibbles"` implements a custom function `deg_min_color()` to demonstrate how to colorize parts of column values. This mechanism is applied to all columns of a given class. So it leads me to conclude that I need to write custom functions for each column class.

However, if I implement a custom `pillar_shaft.numeric()`, it misses all the fun stuff that happens inside the (hidden) `pillar:::pillar_shaft_number()`. Same for `pillar:::pillar_shaft.character()`.

Finally, I see `new_pillar_shaft()` can accept ANSI escape codes in argument `formatted`, however I don't see how to provide ANSI formatting of my own.

Ideal world, I'd like to pass an optional colorization function... somewhere. :)

Thank you for any guidance!

title: Deprecating `...` in `format.tbl` inhibts custom arguments to `print` generic
description:
*Disclaimer*: [I posted this first on SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79433721/extending-tbl-with-custom-print) but I really think the discussion should be happening here.

With the changes introduced in [pillar 1.10.0](https://pillar.r-lib.org/news/index.html#pillar-1100) `...` must now be empty in printing and formatting. 

I am now, however, wondering, how one would allow additional arguments in `print` to be properly handled. Here's a motivating example:

```r
mt <- tibble::new_tibble(mtcars[1:3, ], my_attr = "set", class = "my_tibble")

tbl_format_setup.my_tibble <- function(x, ..., show_attr = TRUE) {
  setup <- NextMethod()
  if (show_attr) {
    setup$tbl_sum <- c(setup$tbl_sum, "Attribute" = attr(x, "my_attr"))
  }
  setup
}
```

Overloading `tbl_format_setup` should enable the user to opt-out from printing the additional line. However, this information must be passed down to the function somehow. Pre 1.10 we could simply use the ellipsis from `print`:

```r
print(mt, show_attr = FALSE)
```

This still works but throws the warning.

I think it is a valid use-case to add some more sub-class specific arguments to `print` and let the underlying workhorse functions handle them appropriately. To avoid the warning altogether, I have to make a clone of `print.tbl` which does not call `format_tbl` directly anymore, but where I copy and paste the code from `format_tbl` undoing the ellipsis check. 

So I either I am overlooking the obvious, or this change actively wants to stop us from adding custom arguments to `print`. Thus, some clarification would be really helpful (even if it is *yes, we do not want you morons to add arguments to print for this and that reason* ;) )

title: Why do `new_pillar_shaft()` and `new_pillar_shaft_simple()` default `min_width` to `width`?
description:
In bench, there is a custom expression class called `bench_expr` that displays the captured expressions

We have a `pillar_shaft()` method for this that looks like:

```r
pillar_shaft.bench_expr <- function(x, ...) {
  pillar::new_pillar_shaft_simple(format.bench_expr(x), align = "left", ...)
}
```

It seems like the way we defined this method is actually the cause of this issue
https://github.com/r-lib/bench/issues/94

i.e. if you have a very long bench expression then it won't get truncated like a normal character column would. It seems like this is because `min_width` defaults to `width`, disallowing any truncation.

It seems like I can fix it by doing this:

```r
pillar_shaft.bench_expr <- function(x, ...) {
  pillar::pillar_shaft(format.bench_expr(x), ...)
}
```

i.e. convert to character and then use the standard `pillar_shaft.character()` method.

The `pillar_shaft.character()` method respects `pillar.min_chars` through `get_pillar_option_min_chars()` so the `min_width` ends up being a good default of `3` by doing this.

I wonder if the default of `new_pillar_shaft()` and `new_pillar_shaft_simple()` should also respect this option rather than defaulting to `width`?

title: df-cols are hidden before any other columns, which feels wrong

title: Feature Request : option to hide temporary columns based on a prefix
description:
Hi, and thanks for your great work on {tibble} and {pillar}.

In my daily workflow, I often create intermediate non-informative columns used only during processing steps (temporary variables, helper columns for joins, reshaping, etc.). 
To clearly mark them as such, I prefix their names with a `.`. 
This helps keep things tidy and indicates these variables are not meant for display or interpretation.

However, when printing a tibble, these columns clutter the output even though they are not useful for human interpretation. 

I'd like to propose a feature where such columns could be hidden by default from the print output, based on a configurable prefix : 

```r 
options(pillar.hide_column_prefix = ".")
```

This would make the output more readable without losing data.

I could override `print.tbl_df()` in my code, but that would be very hacky and not maintainable.

## Notes

- Of course, this should be opt-in and have no impact on default behavior.
- I'm not 100% sure "." is the best prefix (maybe `..`, `_`, or even `tmp_` ?). 
Ultimately, this is up to the user, but I'd be happy to get your opinion about this.
- Maybe an argument in `print()` to opt-out would be nice : `df |> print(n=Inf, print_all=TRUE)`


Thanks again for considering this!

title: Rework printing of control characters
description:
based on ideas in https://github.com/r-lib/pillar/pull/213#issuecomment-716992284:

- Only add quotes if we have space at the beginning or at the end, don't treat internal backslashes any special (if we don't have other weird stuff in the string)
- Highlight control characters in red
- Two output modes: simple and weird
    - simple: no control characters, no ~~double quotes~~`)"`, no spaces at the beginning or end of the text. Simple columns can be copy-pasted into a new-style string literal of the form `r"(text)"` .
    - weird: anything else. Weird cells have quotes and can be used as a string literal directly.

description:
It would be beneficial to have an option `pillar.round` to control the rounding of numbers that straddle 0 - 1.

In the following example the `straddle` column has been subject to rounding as `pillar.sigfig = 3` by default:

```r
library("tidyverse")
#> ── Attaching packages ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse 1.2.1 ──
#> ✔ ggplot2 2.2.1     ✔ purrr   0.2.4
#> ✔ tibble  1.4.2     ✔ dplyr   0.7.4
#> ✔ tidyr   0.8.0     ✔ stringr 1.2.0
#> ✔ readr   1.1.1     ✔ forcats 0.2.0
#> ── Conflicts ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
#> ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
#> ✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
my_numbers <-  c(233, 486, 565, 785)
straddle_data <- tibble(
  big = 1000 * my_numbers + 23,
  stradle = my_numbers / 1000 + 100,
  small = my_numbers / 100000
)
straddle_data
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>      big straddle   small
#>    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 233023     100 0.00233
#> 2 486023     100 0.00486
#> 3 565023     101 0.00565
#> 4 785023     101 0.00785
```

In order to display the fractional component of `straddle`  straddle we need to massively pad the `small` column with `pillar.sigfig = 7`

```r
options(pillar.sigfig = 7)
straddle_data
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>      big straddle       small
#>    <dbl>    <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 233023  100.233 0.002330000
#> 2 486023  100.486 0.004860000
#> 3 565023  100.565 0.005650000
#> 4 785023  100.785 0.007850000
```

It would be useful for the following to work (note the use of \*233\* to indicate the portion of the output that is highlighted thanks to `pillar.subtle = TRUE`) 

```r
options(pillar.round = FALSE)
straddle_data
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>      big straddle       small
#>    <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 *233*023      *100*.233 0.00*233*
#> 2 *486*023      *100*.486 0.00*486*
#> 3 *565*023      *100*.565 0.00*565*
#> 4 *785*023      *100*.785 0.00*785*
```
I appreciate the comment from @hadley here https://github.com/r-lib/pillar/issues/40#issuecomment-360152576 about using a trailing `.` but I think this is a different problem to what was discussed in that issue.

title: Adaptive rendering doesn't fully work
description:
I am following the `latlon` example in [Printing vectors nicely in tibbles](https://vctrs.r-lib.org/articles/pillar.html).
In particular, I want to do [adaptive rendering](https://vctrs.r-lib.org/articles/pillar.html#adaptive-rendering-1).

In my real example, I have a character vector of ugly strings that mean almost nothing to humans (Google Drive file ids, but think: Git commit SHAs or similar).
If there is any sort of horizontal space shortage, this column should be heavily truncated. However I don't, in general, want to truncate this object. I don't want to truncate in a format method. Only inside a tibble.

I'll use the toy `foo` class to demonstrate.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(vctrs)
library(pillar)

new_foo <- function(x = character()) {
  vec_assert(x, character())
  new_vctr(x, class = "foo")
}

data <- tibble(
  month = month.name[1:3],
  sentences = new_foo(stringr::sentences[1:3]),
  blah = stringr::sentences[4:6]
)
data
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>   month   sentences                                   blah                      
#>   <chr>   <foo>                                       <chr>                     
#> 1 January The birch canoe slid on the smooth planks.  These days a chicken leg …
#> 2 Februa… Glue the sheet to the dark blue background. Rice is often served in r…
#> 3 March   It's easy to tell the depth of a well.      The juice of lemons makes…
print(data, width = 60)

#> 3 March  It's easy to tell the depth of a well.      The ju…
```

Here we see that the `foo` column is hogging all the space, because it never gets truncated, because I haven't implemented any methods that would allow this.

If I implement a `pillar_shaft` method as the vignette shows, I do, in fact get truncation. However the horizontal space gained isn't  redistributed to the other columns.

``` r
pillar_shaft.foo <- function(x, ...) {
  full <- format(x)
  trunc <- format(paste0(substr(x, 1, 7), cli::symbol$continue))
  pillar::new_pillar_shaft(
    list(full = full, trunc = trunc),
    width = pillar::get_max_extent(full),
    min_width = pillar::get_max_extent(trunc),
    class = "pillar_shaft_foo"
  )
}

format.pillar_shaft_foo <- function(x, width, ...) {
  if (pillar::get_max_extent(x$full) <= width) {
    ornament <- x$full
  } else {
    ornament <- x$trunc
  }

  pillar::new_ornament(ornament, align = "left")
}

data
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>   month    sentences                             blah                              
#>   <chr>    <foo>                                 <chr>                             
#> 1 January  The bir…                              These days a chicken leg is a rar…
#> 2 February Glue th…                              Rice is often served in round bow…
#> 3 March    It's ea…                              The juice of lemons makes fine pu…
print(data, width = 60)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3

#> 1 January The bir…                    These days a chicken …
#> 2 Februa… Glue th…                    Rice is often served …
#> 3 March   It's ea…                    The juice of lemons m…
```

Having poked around a bit, it seems like the logic in `colonnade_distribute_space_df()` isn't really taking advantage of the fact that the `foo` column only has width 8 if it is truncated at all.

Is there any way for me to do this?

title: Scale Numbers In Columns Equally
description:
This is similar to #41, with the added constraints that the same scale should be picked for all numbers in a column.  Columns that would get this treatment are columns that have large (>= 1e5 in magnitude) or small numbers, or a range that spans more than a couple of orders of magnitude, particularly if it involves numbers that start on both sides of the decimal mark.

Here is an example from a **[twitter post](https://twitter.com/BrodieGaslam/status/954395715270250497)** from last week:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6105908/35392396-b7ec345a-01af-11e8-98fc-1765412d9293.png)

The idea is to make the absolute magnitude and relative magnitude of numbers graspable at a glance.  
I believe this does it with minimal clutter.  `pillar` has the added benefit of the sub-headers, so you could use:

```
 column
<dbl:K>
   1234
```

One key difference with current `pillar` concepts is that we think in terms of significance for the column as a whole, not just a single number.  So if a column contains 1e+9, and 100 as numbers, the first three digits of 100 are not actually significant.  In some cases this will be wrong, but in the bulk of use cases it should be the right way to look at it as numbers in a column are typically the result of the observation of one process with one (repeated) measurement method (with presumably fixed significance and precision for all measurements, respectively).

If you are okay with the loss of precision in the display of significant digits (i.e. we are no longer highlighting exactly 3, but between 3 and 5) then this saves the possibility of using color for other purposes.

As always I'm happy to contribute code if this is something you're interested in.

This all working quite well, but unfortunately pillar seems to be ignoring the `format` function I wrote for the type, and displays the vctrs as the matrix it is internally:

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(tibble)

post <- function(x=matrix(, nrow=0, ncol=0)){
  if(is.vector(x)){
    x <- as.matrix(x)
  }
  stopifnot(is.matrix(x))
  
  new_vctr(c(x), nsamples=ncol(x), dim=c(nrow(x), ncol(x)), class="post")
}

  matrix(vec_data(x), ncol=attr(x, "nsamples"))
}

  rowMeans(as.matrix(x))
}
obj_print_footer.post <- function(x, ...) {

}
```

@hadley: Do we initiate soft-deprecation now? It seems safe -- it's only a message once per session, and also only for direct callers.

title: List columns of rcrd type don't display size of each element
description:
I'm slightly confused about if this is caused by `vctrs`, `pillar` or `tibble`, but found a very similar issue in this repo (https://github.com/r-lib/pillar/issues/167). Also, this might just be expected behavior, so please feel free to close if I'm mistaken.

In the reprex below, I create a tibble with a list column of `rational` vectors. I'd expect each row to be printed like `<rtnl [5]>` but they are instead printed like `<rtnl>`.

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(zeallot)

new_rational <- function(n = integer(), d = integer()) {
  vec_assert(n, ptype = integer())
  vec_assert(d, ptype = integer())
  
  new_rcrd(list(n = n, d = d), class = "vctrs_rational")
}

rational <- function(n, d) {
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_cast_common(n, d, .to = integer())
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_recycle_common(n, d)
  
  new_rational(n, d)
}

format.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) {
  n <- field(x, "n")
  d <- field(x, "d")
  
  out <- paste0(n, "/", d)
  out[is.na(n) | is.na(d)] <- NA
  
  out
}

vec_ptype_abbr.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) "rtnl"
vec_ptype_full.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) "rational"

# doesn't show size of each vector
tibble::tibble(x = list(rational(1, 1:10), rational(1, 1:2)))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>   x     
#>   <list>
#> 1 <rtnl>
#> 2 <rtnl>

# do show size of each vector
tibble::tibble(x = list(1:5, hms::hms(1:5)))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>   x         
#>   <list>    
#> 1 <int [5]> 
#> 2 <time [5]>
```

title: Don't print decimals if no value in vector has decimals.
description:
When importing data from other software packages into R (e.g. from Stata, SAS or SPSS, using *haven*), vector are of type _double_, even if they are integers.

Would you mind checking if a vector has "floating point" values, or are actually "interger-doubles", and then omit the decimals? (something like `is.numeric(x) && !all(x %% 1 == 0, na.rm = T)`)

Current output:
``` r
library(tibble)
tibble(a = c(1, 2, 3), b = c(1L, 2L, 3L))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>       a     b
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1  1.00     1
#> 2  2.00     2
#> 3  3.00     3
```

Since all values in `a` are "integers", the desired output would be like column `b`. The problem is, that this is a guess, if it's a double or probably was intended as integer. But I can think of (new) R users being confused when they see their values in the SPSS data sheet as "integers", and in the R console as doubles.

title: TRUE and FALSE, not T and F
description:
I suggest displaying logical `TRUE` and `FALSE` as just that, vs. `T` and `F`.

I think many discourage the use of `T` and `F` in code, when we mean `TRUE` and `FALSE`, so I don't like giving the suboptimal thing so much exposure.

Also, as @hadley points out, `<lgl>` and `FALSE` are the same width, so `T` and `F` aren't actually saving any horizontal space.

title: bugs with non-default pillar.sigfig settings
description:
Depending on where the decimal point falls, the `pillar.sigfig` option sometimes does not work correctly when set to a non-default value.

Here is the result with the default setting, which works as expected:
```
> pillar::pillar(c(1234.56, 123.456, 12.3456, 1.23456, 0.123456))
   <dbl>
1235    
 123    
  12.3  
   1.23 
   0.123
```

title: Can pillar_shaft.POSIXt() respect the digits.secs option?
description:
I think it would be nice if `pillar_shaft.POSIXt()` printed `POSIXct` objects in the same way as base R, respecting `getOption("digits.secs")`. This is mainly useful for printing fractional seconds, which aren't currently shown at any time in the current implementation.

The following seems to work well enough for me:

```r
pillar_shaft.POSIXt <- function(x, ...) {
  
  # Get the value of the option, default is 0
  fractional       <- getOption("digits.secs")
  # The width needs to be adjusted. If we are printing fractional seconds, adjust
  # by adding the number of fractional seconds to print +1 for the decimal, otherwise do nothing.
  fractional_width <- ifelse(fractional, fractional + 1, 0)
  
  date <- format(x, format = "%Y-%m-%d")

  # Use the "%OS" format to print. When we don't use any fractional seconds, I believe
  # "%OS0" is equivalent to "%S"
  time <- format(x, format = paste0("%H:%M:%OS", fractional))
  
  datetime <- paste0(date, " " , style_subtle(time))
  datetime[is.na(x)] <- NA
  
  # Add to the width
  new_pillar_shaft_simple(datetime, width = 19 + fractional_width, align = "left")
}
```

title: Column spacing is incorrect when printing columns with fractional seconds
description:
Following discussion on #74. When the user sets `digits.secs` option, the fractional seconds are printed but the spacing is off because `width` is not adjusted dynamically. The reprex below outlines the problem and proposes a solution.

``` r
# with dev pillar and tibble
library(pillar)
library(tibble)

from <- as.POSIXct("14:03:55", format="%H:%M:%OS", tz="UTC")
to   <- as.POSIXct("14:04:00", format="%H:%M:%OS", tz="UTC")

options(digits.secs = 4)

ex <- tibble(datetime = seq(from, to, by = 0.01))

ex$col <- 100000

# The correct amount of spacing is not used with fractional seconds
print(ex, n = 2)
#> # A tibble: 501 x 2
#>   datetime                col
#>   <dttm>                <dbl>
#> 1 2018-03-01 14:03:55.0000 100000.
#> 2 2018-03-01 14:03:55.0099 100000.
#> # ... with 499 more rows

# Potential solution
# This should really be pillar_shaft.POSIXt but had to do this for testing
# FYI the digits.secs option allows values from 0-6 and defaults to NULL (0)
pillar_shaft.POSIXct <- function (x, ...) 
{
  # Fractional seconds width adjustment
  width <- 19L
  digits.secs <- min(max(getOption("digits.secs"), 0L), 6L) # Clamp between 0-6
  if (digits.secs) {
    width <- width + digits.secs + 1L # The 1L is for the extra decimal point
  } 
  
  date <- format(x, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
  time <- format(x, format = "%H:%M:%OS")
  datetime <- paste0(date, " ", style_subtle(time))
  datetime[is.na(x)] <- NA
  new_pillar_shaft_simple(datetime, width = width, align = "left")
}

print(ex, n = 2)
#> # A tibble: 501 x 2
#>   datetime                     col
#>   <dttm>                     <dbl>
#> 1 2018-03-01 14:03:55.0000 100000.
#> 2 2018-03-01 14:03:55.0099 100000.
#> # ... with 499 more rows

# Even if the user does something crazy everything is alright...

# The default 
options(digits.secs = NULL)
head(ex, n = 1)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   datetime                col
#>   <dttm>                <dbl>
#> 1 2018-03-01 14:03:55 100000.

#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
```

title: Decide on vctrs use
description:
pillar 1.4.0 imports the vctrs package, primarily to support the `vec_ptype_abbr()` generic. It's also using the following functions:

- `vec_is()` (only available in the dev version)
- `vec_dim()`

The cyclic dependency between vctrs and pillar causes some problems down the line: vctrs registers methods for generics that are defined in pillar, namely `type_sum()` and `pillar_shaft()`.

The current dev version of vctrs no longer registers these methods after https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/338 (this is done by the current dev version of pillar). The problems caused by the cyclic dependency seem to appear only with dev vctrs, the recent fixes should take care of this. CRAN vctrs + pillar already works fine, so should CRAN vctrs + dev pillar.

We should decide if:

- [ ] we keep importing vctrs (clearly being aware of its experimental nature)
- [ ] we keep forwarding `type_sum()` to `vec_ptype_abbr()` or reinstantiate `type_sum()` methods for all objects
- [ ] we keep using `vec_is()` and `vec_dim()` or revert to internal implementations for now

CC @lionel- @hadley.

title: `list_of()` in list-columns doesn't display `vec_size()` correctly for record type
description:
Sorry for opening a new issue regarding #442 . I have rephrased the title to reflect the issue better, instead of feature requesting for `obj_print_size()`.

The example of record type is taken from the vignette https://vctrs.r-lib.org/articles/s3-vector.html#rational-class 

``` r
library(vctrs)

new_rational <- function(n = integer(), d = integer()) {
  vec_assert(n, ptype = integer())
  vec_assert(d, ptype = integer())
  
  new_rcrd(list(n = n, d = d), class = "vctrs_rational")
}

rational <- function(n, d) {
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_cast_common(n, d, .to = integer())
  c(n, d) %<-% vec_recycle_common(n, d)
  
  new_rational(n, d)
}

format.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) {
  n <- field(x, "n")
  d <- field(x, "d")
  
  out <- paste0(n, "/", d)
  out[is.na(n) | is.na(d)] <- NA
  
  out
}

vec_ptype_abbr.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) "rtnl"
vec_ptype_full.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) "rational"

x <- rational(1, 1:10)
x
#> <rational[10]>
#>  [1] 1/1  1/2  1/3  1/4  1/5  1/6  1/7  1/8  1/9  1/10
vec_size(x)
#> [1] 10
```

The `vec_size()` works perfectly for the underlying size. My issue with record type is related to `list_of()` when using it in the list-column. I'd expect `[50]` to be displayed in the `ratio` list-column instead of `[2]`. Printing the full `list_of` shows `<vctrs_rcrd[50]>`, which is as expected.

```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  summarise(
    ratio = list_of(rational(as.integer(Sepal.Length), as.integer(Sepal.Width)))
  )
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   Species           ratio
#>   <fct>      <list<rtnl>>
#> 1 setosa              [2]
#> 2 versicolor          [2]
#> 3 virginica           [2]

iris %>% 
  vec_split(iris$Species) %>% 
  pull(val) %>% 
  purrr::map(~ rational(as.integer(.$Sepal.Length), as.integer(.$Sepal.Width))) %>% 
  as_list_of()
#> <list_of<rational>[3]>
#> [[1]]
#> <vctrs_rcrd[50]>
#> `format.vctrs_rcrd()` not implemented.
```

The aside issue is that `as_list_of()` appears to lose the class `vctrs_rational`.
